[1] The bell above the door had been replaced. Corinne noticed that before she noticed anything else—before the smell of machine oil and lemon polish, before the wall of clocks ticking out of step with one another, before the man at the bench in the back who did not look up. The old bell had been brass and had rung flat, like a spoon dropped in a sink. This one was bright and even, and it seemed to her an unreasonable thing to have changed.

[2] "We close at five," Walter said, still bent over whatever was in front of him. He had a loupe screwed into one eye and a pair of tweezers in his right hand, and the hand was steady. She had half expected it not to be.

[3] "It's ten past four," she said.

[4] The tweezers stopped. He did not turn around, but she watched his shoulders do something complicated—rise, hold, settle—as if he were lifting a weight he had set down years ago and had hoped never to pick up again. Then he took the loupe out of his eye and laid it on the felt, and turned on the stool, and looked at her.

[5] "So it is," he said.

[6] She had rehearsed several openings on the drive up the coast, and all of them abandoned her now. What she said instead was, "You changed the bell."

[7] "The other one cracked." He said it as though it had happened last week, though she could see from the tarnish on the mounting screws that it had been longer than that. "Kept ringing anyway. Sounded worse every year. Finally I thought, a person ought not to have to listen to that."

[8] "I liked it."

[9] "You would." There was no unkindness in it. He stood, slowly, one hand flat on the bench, and she saw that he was shorter than she remembered, or that she was taller, or that memory had simply been generous. "You'll want coffee. Kettle's where it was."

[10] It was. So was the tin of grounds, and so, on the shelf above the sink, was the blue mug with the chip out of its handle—the one she had dropped on the flagstones the summer she was nine and had cried over as if it were a living thing. She had assumed he'd thrown it out. She took it down and filled it and did not say anything about it, and neither did he, though when she came back into the front room with it he glanced at the mug and then away, and she understood that he had seen her see it.

[11] "Business good?" she asked.

[12] "Nobody fixes anything anymore. They buy new." He shrugged. "But the ones who do come, they come a long way. I had a fellow from Halifax in March with a carriage clock his grandmother brought over. Two months I had that thing apart." He nodded toward the wall, where a dozen pendulums swung at their own private tempos. "Most of those are waiting on parts I have to make myself."

[13] She drank the coffee, which was terrible in exactly the way she remembered. Outside, a gull landed on the sill and regarded them both through the glass with one yellow eye. Walter went back to the bench, but he did not put the loupe back in. He picked up a small brass wheel and turned it over in his fingers, examining nothing.

[14] "I saw the notice," she said finally. "In the paper. About the building."

[15] "Ah." He set the wheel down. "That's why."

[16] "That's not why."

[17] He let it go, which she had not expected. In the old days he would have pressed the point until one of them left the room, and it had usually been her, and the door had usually made the bell ring its flat cracked note behind her. "They want to put up condominiums," he said. "Glass and steel, right out to the seawall. Your mother would have written letters. I don't write letters."

[18] "I could."

[19] He looked at her a long moment. On the wall the clocks reached the quarter hour in a ragged volley of chimes, none of them agreeing, and he waited for them to finish before he answered, as he had always waited, as though the clocks had a right to speak first.

[20] "You still have the key?" he said.

[21] She did. It was on the ring in her pocket, between the key to an apartment three hundred miles away and the key to a car she no longer owned. She had never once used it since the day she left, and she had never once taken it off.

[22] "Good," Walter said, and put the loupe back in his eye. "Then you can lock up. I'll be a while with this."

Two people long apart approach each other indirectly, through familiar objects and routines rather than open conversation.

correct_answer: Two people long apart approach each other indirectly, through familiar objects and routines rather than open conversation.
explanation: Nothing is being repaired for Corinne, no sale is proposed, and the two never argue about modernizing anything. Every exchange—the bell, the mug, the coffee, the key—circles the long absence without naming it, which is the shape of the whole scene.

passage_title: The Gap Between Intending and Doing
passage:
[1] Every January, gyms in the United States sign up more new members than in any other month, and every February a large share of those members stop coming. The people who sign up are not insincere. Surveys consistently find that they intend to exercise and expect to keep going. What separates the ones who do from the ones who do not has become one of the central questions in the study of habit.

[2] Psychologists call the phenomenon the intention-behavior gap. For decades, models of behavior change assumed that if you could persuade people to want to do something, the doing would follow. Public-health campaigns were designed on that assumption, and many of them succeeded in changing what people said they wanted while leaving what they did almost untouched. A person can know, believe, and intend, and still find at six in the morning that the alarm is easier to silence than to obey.

[3] The research that followed shifted attention away from wanting and toward circumstance. In one study, researchers tracked more than a thousand new members of a university recreation center over their first twelve weeks. Stated motivation at sign-up turned out to be a weak predictor of attendance. Much stronger were mundane details: how far the member lived from the building, whether they had a regular time slot, and whether they went with someone else. Members who came at the same hour on the same days, even if they came less often at first, were far more likely to still be attending at week twelve than members who came whenever they felt like it.

[4] "Motivation gets you through the door once," says Dr. Ama Osei, a behavioral scientist who studies routine formation. "It does not get you through the door the fortieth time. By then, if the behavior is going to survive, something in the environment has to be doing the work that willpower was doing at the start." That "something," in Osei's account, is a cue: a consistent feature of the situation—a time of day, a location, a preceding action—that comes to trigger the behavior automatically. Habits, on this view, are not strong intentions. They are associations between contexts and actions, built by repetition until the context alone is enough.

[5] The distinction has practical consequences. If habits live in contexts, then disrupting the context should disrupt the habit—and it does. Studies of people who move to a new city find that established routines tend to dissolve in the weeks after the move, because the cues that sustained them are gone. The same disruption creates an opening. People who take up a new behavior shortly after relocating are more likely to keep it than people who attempt the same change while their surroundings stay fixed, presumably because the new behavior is not competing with an old one that the environment keeps prompting.

[6] Researchers have also found that people are more likely to attempt a change at moments that feel like beginnings: a new year, a birthday, a Monday. These "temporal landmarks" appear to work partly by separating a person's sense of who they are now from who they were before, which makes the old pattern feel like someone else's. The effect is real but modest, and it fades quickly. A landmark helps a behavior begin. It does nothing to keep it going.

[7] What does keep it going, the evidence suggests, is friction—or rather its absence. Small obstacles have outsized effects on whether a behavior is repeated. In one experiment, an office cafeteria moved a water dispenser from a corner to a spot next to the checkout and saw water consumption rise sharply, with no change in prices, signage, or the availability of other drinks. The reverse holds as well: adding a single extra step to a routine, such as requiring a key card to enter a room, measurably reduces how often people use the room.

[8] These findings have made their way into policy. Retirement savings plans that enroll employees automatically, and require them to opt out rather than opt in, achieve participation rates far higher than plans that ask people to sign up, even though the plans themselves are identical. Nobody's intentions about saving changed; the default did. Critics of this approach argue that arranging environments to steer behavior treats adults as objects to be nudged rather than as agents making choices, and that a person who saves only because a form was pre-filled has not really chosen anything. Defenders reply that there is no neutral arrangement—some default always exists—and that the question is only whether it is set with people's stated goals in mind or against them.

[9] Osei is less interested in the policy debate than in the individual. "People blame themselves when a resolution fails," she says. "They conclude they lack discipline. Usually the more accurate conclusion is that they tried to change a behavior without changing anything around it." The gap between intending and doing, on this reading, is not a character flaw. It is a design problem, and design problems can be solved.

[1] The first time I sat in with a real band, I was seventeen and I had learned every solo on three records note for note. I could play them in my sleep; I sometimes did. I played my licks anyway. They were in tune and in time and they had nothing to do with what was happening around me. Afterward the drummer, who was sixty and kind, told me, "You played beautifully. You just weren't here."

[2] I have spent forty years trying to be here. That is what improvisation is, for me: not invention out of nothing, which is impossible, but attention. The material—the scales, the voicings, the phrases picked up from a hundred other players—is real, and I would never pretend I made it up. But the material is only vocabulary. Conversation is not vocabulary. Conversation is what happens when someone says something you did not expect and you have to answer with what you have, in the time you have, in front of everyone. I can hear the difference in myself on a bad night: the hands running the old routes while the ears have gone somewhere else.

[3] People who do not play sometimes ask whether it is frightening. It is, and it should be. The fear is information. It tells you that you do not know what is coming, which is the only condition under which listening is necessary. The night the fear leaves is the night you have started playing your records again instead of listening to the room. I have heard great musicians do it, late in their careers—reach for the thing that worked in 1974 because it worked in 1974—and the audience applauds, because the thing is still beautiful. But the other players on the stand know. They can feel that the door has closed.

[4] What I want to say to the seventeen-year-old is this: learn everything, and then go somewhere you can't use it. Find a bass player who asks questions. The records will always be there. The room will not. That is the whole lesson, and it took me half a lifetime to learn it.

[1] There is a story jazz tells about itself, and it goes like this: the improviser walks onto the stand with nothing but an instrument and an open heart, and what comes out has never existed before and will never exist again. It is a beautiful story. It is also, as anyone who has transcribed a great many solos can tell you, mostly untrue. Listeners want to believe it; players, who should know better, often believe it too.

[2] Analyze the recorded improvisations of any celebrated player and you find a finite set of phrases—perhaps a few hundred—recurring across years of performances, transposed, reordered, and stitched together with a fluency that can look like spontaneous creation to a listener who has not heard the seams. Once you have heard them you cannot stop hearing them, and the solos do not become less beautiful for it. This is not a scandal. It is how every improvised art works, from oral epic to stand-up comedy. Fluency is built from formulas. The ancient bard did not invent his stock epithets fresh each night; he reached for them because they fit the meter, and his artistry lay in the reaching.

[3] What troubles me is not the formulas but the mythology that hides them, because the mythology damages musicians. Young players are taught to worship an ideal of pure spontaneity that no one, including their heroes, has ever met. When they discover, as they must, that their own playing is built from borrowed parts, they conclude they are frauds. I have sat with such players. [1] On a summer afternoon, two neighborhoods a few kilometers apart in the same city can differ in air temperature by five degrees Celsius or more. The hotter one is rarely hotter by accident. Cities are warmer than the countryside around them—a pattern known as the urban heat island—but the warmth is not spread evenly. It concentrates where the ground has been paved, where buildings are dense and low, and where trees are scarce. Understanding why has become urgent as heat waves grow longer and more frequent, because the neighborhoods that run hottest are often the ones whose residents have the fewest ways to escape the heat.

[2] The physics begins with what happens to sunlight when it reaches the ground. A surface can reflect it, absorb it, or use it to evaporate water. Bare asphalt reflects little and evaporates nothing; it absorbs most of the energy that falls on it, warms to temperatures that can exceed 60°C on a hot day, and releases that stored heat slowly through the evening and night. This is why cities cool so little after dark: the heat absorbed by pavement and masonry during the day keeps radiating for hours. A grass lawn absorbs sunlight too, but it also moves water from the soil into the air through its leaves, and every gram of water evaporated carries away energy that would otherwise have become heat.

[3] Trees do this on a larger scale and add a second effect: shade. A mature tree's canopy intercepts sunlight before it reaches the ground, so the surface beneath never accumulates the heat that an exposed surface would. Measurements under a dense canopy at midday routinely show surface temperatures fifteen to twenty degrees below those of adjacent pavement in full sun. Meanwhile the leaves themselves are transpiring, cooling the air that passes through the crown. The two effects reinforce each other, and their combined result is that tree cover is among the strongest single predictors of how hot a neighborhood becomes.

[4] It is not the only one. The share of ground covered by impervious surfaces—roads, roofs, parking lots—matters independently, because it determines how much of the sunlight that does reach the ground is stored rather than dissipated. Two neighborhoods with the same canopy cover can differ noticeably in temperature if one has more exposed pavement between the trees. Building geometry matters as well: narrow streets flanked by tall buildings trap heat in what researchers call urban canyons, while also casting shade that can reduce daytime surface temperatures. And proximity to water bodies moderates temperature swings, since water warms and cools more slowly than land.

[5] Researchers investigating one mid-sized city selected five residential neighborhoods with similar housing density and measured, for each, the percentage of land under tree canopy, the percentage under impervious surface, and the mean land-surface temperature at 2 p.m. across ten cloudless days in July. Their results are summarized in the table below.

Table 1. Five neighborhoods, July measurements
Neighborhood | Tree canopy (%) | Impervious surface (%) | Mean surface temp., 2 p.m. (°C)
Elmwood Heights | 38 | 31 | 33.1
Riverside | 22 | 40 | 34.0
Fairview | 21 | 55 | 38.2
Central | 9 | 71 | 41.6
Harbor Flats | 6 | 68 | 39.4

[6] The broad pattern is what the physics predicts: as canopy falls and pavement rises, temperature climbs. But the table also shows the limits of any single variable. Two of the neighborhoods have nearly identical canopy cover yet differ by more than four degrees, a gap the researchers attributed largely to the difference in impervious surface between them. And the neighborhood with the least canopy of all was not the hottest. Harbor Flats, which sits along the waterfront, ran more than two degrees cooler than Central despite having less tree cover and a comparable share of pavement—the moderating effect of the water, the researchers concluded, was offsetting what the neighborhood lacked in shade.

[7] Findings like these shape how cities respond. Planting trees is the most visible intervention and, over decades, one of the most effective, but a sapling casts almost no shade, and a canopy that lowers surface temperatures by several degrees takes twenty or thirty years to grow. In the meantime, cities have turned to faster measures: coating roofs and pavement with reflective materials that absorb less sunlight, replacing asphalt with permeable surfaces that hold water and allow evaporation, and preserving the mature trees that already exist, since a single large tree provides more cooling than dozens of newly planted ones.

[8] The last point is the one researchers stress most. Canopy is easy to lose and slow to replace, and the neighborhoods that have the least of it today are frequently the ones where it was cleared for road widening or parking decades ago. Restoring it is possible, but the map of where a city is hottest is, in large part, a map of decisions made long before the current heat wave arrived.
